description: Somos un equipo enfocado en crear una experiencia educativa e interactiva sobre misiones espaciales. Buscamos personas con interés en programación, diseño, ciencia, 3D y gamificación para desarrollar juntos un MVP competitivo para NASA Space Apps.
summary: Space lessons for kids are often posters full of facts, or too technical to feel real. Mars Mission X is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) browser game for children aged 7–12. Guided by Paqo, an astronaut alpaca, players run a small Mars base for five sols. Each sol the Sun gives a few energy tokens, and players decide where they go: the air machine, the water recycler, greenhouse lamps for lettuce and potatoes, a radiation shield, or the antenna that lets Earth's warnings arrive in time. There is never enough energy for everything, so every choice is a real trade-off between life support, food, protection and communication. Solar storms are real NASA DONKI events, the units come from NASA life-support data, and every source is shown in the game. A mission card, a guided first sol, colour-coded goals and a "Help me, Paqo!" button make sure nobody gets stuck, and running out is never punishing: Paqo explains why and the player tries again. Every mission is different, so kids replay and test new strategies.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Players tap the buildings of a 2.5D Mars base to zoom inside and give them energy. Each sol has 10 energy tokens in Commander mode or 12 in the easier Explorer mode (7 on a dust-storm sol in both). Four astronauts need 1 unit of air, 1 of water and 1 portion of food each per sol. The air machine and the water recycler turn energy into air and clean water. In the greenhouse, players plant lettuce (fast: 2 lit sols, 2 portions) or potatoes (slow: 4 lit sols, 5 portions), and each lamp costs 1 token. The shield (2 tokens) protects the crew during a solar storm, and the antenna (1 token) lets Earth's warning arrive one sol early. Radiation is invisible, so without the antenna the storm is a surprise.

WHY IT TEACHES A REAL CONSTRAINT

Keeping air and water steady costs 8 tokens and lighting three pots costs 3 more: 11 tokens for a 10-token day. Players must borrow from reserves, plan crops ahead, and choose between food and protection on storm days, the same kind of trade-off mission planners face. A live preview shows tomorrow's air, water and food before confirming, and a "show real numbers" switch converts units to kilograms for older siblings and teachers.

REAL NASA DATA

One air unit equals the oxygen one astronaut breathes in a sol (0.895 kg, NASA BVAD Rev. 2), and one water unit equals 3.2 kg (BVAD). An end-of-game card explains the ISS's 98% water recovery (NASA, 2023). The dust-storm sol gives about 70% of normal power, close to InSight's 65% in a 2022 regional storm. Solar storms are four real Solar Energetic Particle events from NASA DONKI (May 2024), shown with their date and a link, and clearly labelled as archived, not live. The 3 to 22 minute Earth–Mars radio delay is derived from Mars Fact Sheet distances. End-of-game cards and a "NASA sources" panel show every citation.

KID-FRIENDLY AND REPLAYABLE

Paqo, an astronaut alpaca, speaks every hint aloud in short phrases (Spanish or English) with a repeat button, so early readers can play. There is playful music and a sound for every button, all behind one mute switch. Plain language, big touch targets, a keyboard-accessible interface, reduced-motion support, and no accounts or downloads. Each mission randomly picks the dust-storm day, the solar-storm day and the real DONKI event, and a seed in the URL replays the same mission for a whole class. Failure is a chance to learn: Paqo explains what went wrong and the player repeats the sol; fewer repeats earn more stars, and the game ends with a Junior Astronaut diploma.
We play-tested the game with more than 20 children from our academy. They enjoyed it, and watching where they got confused led us to add the mission card, the guided first sol, the colour-coded goals and the "Help me, Paqo!" button.

NOBODY GETS STUCK

A mission card states the goal before the first sol: every sol the four astronauts use 4 air, 4 water and 4 food; keep all three goals green for five sols. The top bar is the list of goals: each meter turns green, amber or red and spells out the sum in words ("you have 6, +4, they use 4, left 6"). Food turns amber one sol early, when tomorrow's meals are not growing yet. The first sol is guided: Paqo's hand points at one thing at a time and he says each step aloud. If the child tries to end a sol that will fail, Paqo says "Wait!" and shows what is missing. A "Help me, Paqo!" button shares out the day's energy with a plan that keeps the mission winnable, and Paqo explains each choice; it costs one star, so trying alone is still rewarded.

IMMERSIVE BUT LIGHT

The game opens with a countdown, lift-off and Mars landing. Every scene is alive (looping animations, storm clips, a spinning base you can drag), each energy token visibly flies from the solar panels to the machine it powers, and every sol ends with a time-lapse into the Martian night. A Lite mode (still images, no motion) turns on automatically for players who prefer reduced motion.

HOW IT IS BUILT

A pure, deterministic TypeScript engine computes each sol, and the on-screen preview uses the same function. 24 automated tests check the rules; a solver proves every possible mission can be won without repeating a sol, and that Paqo's help always finds a winning plan. Built with React, Vite and TypeScript, tested with Vitest, deployed on GitHub Pages. Open source (MIT).

TRANSPARENCY

Before the event we  built a practice prototype to learn the tools. Following the rule that work on the challenge must happen during the hackathon, this submission was rebuilt from scratch during the event in a new repository; the commit history shows the timeline. A planning document was prepared beforehand.
